title: CytoMed Therapeutics completes cash acquisition of Cord Blood Banking Licence and Assets expanding CytoMed’s strategy to cord blood-derived biologics through subsidiary, LongevityBank
body_text: SINGAPORE, Oct. 03, 2024 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CytoMed Therapeutics Limited (NASDAQ: GDTC) (“CytoMed” or “Company”), a Singapore-based biopharmaceutical company focused on harnessing its proprietary technologies to develop novel donor blood-derived, cell-based allogeneic therapies for the treatment of various cancers and aging-related diseases, has through its subsidiary, IPSC Depository Sdn Bhd, acquired the licence and certain assets of Cellsafe International Sdn Bhd (In Liquidation), a Malaysian cord blood bank. The acquisition includes (i) a cord blood banking licence issued by Malaysia’s Ministry of Health, (ii) cryopreservation equipment with more than 12,000 cord blood units (“CBUs”) and (iii) two freehold real estate properties totalling 189 square metres in which the operation is situated. This acquisition will expand CytoMed’s strategy in cell therapies as it now has access to rare and precious naïve cord blood donated for research and development. There are abundant clinical publications and evidence that cord blood offers a wide range of opportunities in the fields of regenerative medicine and aging diseases, including auto-immune diseases. This new biotechnology arm will be undertaken through CytoMed’s subsidiary, LongevityBank Pte Ltd. The latter is the holding company of IPSC Depository Sdn Bhd which holds the cord blood banking licence issued by the Ministry of Health, Malaysia. Once considered medical waste, cord blood has emerged as a valuable raw material with significant therapeutic potential in cell therapies. However, cord blood is a rare and expensive resource unlike adult blood mononuclear cells, which are readily accessible and a common raw material for researchers. In recent years, researchers have made significant strides in harnessing the unique properties of cord blood derived cells for combating auto-immune diseases and cancer, as well as promoting healthy aging. “This acquisition seeks to unlock the therapeutic potential of umbilical cord blood and adds a new strategic dimension targeting longevity and wellness,” said Evelyn Tan, the newly appointed CEO of IPSC Depository Sdn Bhd. She added “While CytoMed, our publicly listed holding company, will continue to focus on cancer therapeutics, LongevityBank Pte Ltd will focus exclusively on the regenerative medicine market, with its ultimate goal to be spun off in the future.” CytoMed’s co-CEO Dr Tan Wee Kiat added “Mononuclear cells in the CBU are the starting raw material from which many cell therapies can be derived. In addition to longevity targets, there is clear synergy between CytoMed and IPSC Depository to focus on deriving immune gamma delta T cells from cord blood to fight cancers. We own our state-of-the-art, current Good Manufacturing Practice laboratory to ensure quality and cost-control, and have patented technologies to manufacture clinical grade chimeric antigen receptor cells, or CAR-T cells as adjunctive therapies, should the no-option patient’s doctor recommend it.” The Company will be inviting experts in longevity field to join its board of directors or as advisers as it seeks to develop and grow this subsidiary as a specialised umbilical cord blood-derived cell therapy arm. About CytoMed Therapeutics Limited (CytoMed) Incorporated in 2018, CytoMed was spun off from the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore’s leading research and development agency in the public sector. It is a biopharmaceutical company focused on harnessing its licensed proprietary technologies, namely gamma delta T cell and iPSC-derived gamma delta Natural Killer T cell, to create novel cell-based allogeneic immunotherapies for the treatment of various human cancers. The development of novel technologies has been inspired by the clinical success of existing CAR-T therapies in treating haematological malignancies, as well as the current clinical limitations and commercial challenges in extrapolating the CAR-T principle into the treatment of solid tumours. title: Cutting Costs with Clarity: How Transparent PBMs Are Changing the Game for Good
body_text: When it comes to sky-high drug prices, it's easy to point the finger at big pharmaceutical companies. After all, they are the ones developing and selling the medications. What people often don’t know is that the true culprits are Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs). We explain this in more detail in our post “Are you sure you know your PBM? ” This issue is exacerbated by the lack of competition in the industry where the three largest PBMs (CVS Caremark, Optum Rx, and Express Scripts) control 80% of the market . While the government is finally stepping in and proposing bills to aid the severity of this issue, the progress is not fast enough to impact the biggest PBMs anytime soon. So instead, the remaining 20% are taking matters into their own hands, creating a subset of transparent PBMs that are operating with integrity, prioritizing the financial well-being of their clients, and already seeing promising results. For instance, the transparent PBM SmithRx reports that their clients save up to 20% on pharmacy costs, showing that with the right incentives, PBMs still can positively impact drug pricing. As a self-insured employer or benefits consultant, it's crucial to understand this shift. Thus, in this post, we'll explore what makes transparent PBMs different from traditional ones and highlight specific PBMs that exemplify what the industry should strive to be. Let’s dive in! What are transparent PBMs? From the outside, transparent PBM’s are just like the traditional ones. They negotiate discounts and rebates with pharmacies and drug manufacturers to secure lower prices for their clients. The key difference lies in their revenue model. Compared to more traditional PBM’s, transparent PBMs only generate revenue through administration fees, eliminating the main cost drivers– spread pricing and rebate retention. This means that they pass on all negotiated discounts and rebate arrangements to their clients resulting in the decrease in pharmacy spend as reported by SmithRx. We are so excited about what these PBMs are doing! So much so that we had to jump on the transparency bandwagon with our transparent TPA services. You know what they say, if you can't beat 'em, join 'em! We also illustrate this in the diagrams below using the example of our fictional company CoolClaim. As you can see, under the transparent PBM model, the PBM does not charge CoolClaim any hidden fees, generating revenue solely from the agreed upon $10 administration fee. By this, CoolClaim saves $40 compared to the traditional PBM model! ‍ ‍ How are transparent PBMs different from traditional PBMs? Of course, critics could say that the changes in the PBMs’ revenue models could be all talk, no substance. How can clients be sure that they are truly reaping the benefits promised by their PBM? This is where transparency comes into play. Transparent PBMs provide their clients with full access to their pricing structures, fees, and rebate arrangements, including the details of any rebates negotiated with drug manufacturers. They provide this data in real time so that their clients have an up to date understanding of their healthcare expenditures at all times. This means no hidden fees or sneaky pricing tricks! When it comes to tricks, complete transparency also helps clients make more independent cost-effective prescription choices. With transparent PBMs, they won't be tricked into including more expensive drugs in their plan just so the PBMs can earn higher rebates. Instead, they will be able to choose a formulary that is truly the best fit for their employees in terms of accessibility and quality. It's a win-win situation where transparency leads to trust, better health outcomes, and cost savings! Alert: Transparent and pass-through PBMs are NOT the same! There is one thing that we need to clear up before we continue. You might have noticed that, while some sources use "transparent PBMs" and "pass-through PBMs" interchangeably, we have not done that a single time. The reason? Transparent and pass-through are not the same. In fact they differ in the services they offer which is important to understand, especially if you are considering working with one. Pass-through PBMs focus on lowering their client’s pharmacy costs by ensuring that 100% of negotiated discounts and rebates go directly to the patient. Transparent PBMs take it a step further. Not only do they pass all pricing benefits to their clients, but they also offer complete access to their financial and pricing structures. Think of transparent PBMs as the upgraded version of pass-through PBMs, providing full visibility and accountability along with the cost-saving benefits. So, before you make your move towards cutting pharmacy costs, make sure you know exactly who you're hiring to maximize your savings and transparency! Where to start? Transparent PBMs certainly make a compelling case for themselves, but with so many options out there, how do you choose the right one? There's no one-size-fits-all answer, as different PBMs will align better with different client goals and requirements. Yet, to help you kickstart your transparent cost savings journey, we highlighted a few PBM’s that we think are worth checking out (we’re not paid to say any of this, we’re just sharing what we know). These PBMs not only meet the high standards of transparency but also deliver impressive results in reducing pharmacy costs. See for yourself! ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Website: https://www.ehimrx.com/ EHIM is a great option for clients looking for a personalized service. EHIM works with each of their clients to create a custom formulary to help them achieve their goals in the most efficient way. Other PBMs tend to have a set formulary. EHIM also offers a specialty drug solution, “EHIM Cares”, as a part of their services that detects specialty drug savings opportunities, provides more robust criteria for managing specialty medications and offers patients 24/7 nursing and pharmacy support. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ ‍ Website: https://www.pcarx.com/ PCA Rx describes itself as a "full-service PBM that delivers a flexible, high-touch benefit", and they are not wrong! On top of their transparent formulary and pharmacy network management, they also offer medical claim audit services to help their clients monitor instances of medication duplication and offer therapy management services that help patients maximize their medication benefits. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Website: https://www.smithrx.com/ SmithRX are committed to their 100% pass through revenue model that, based on their reports, saves plan sponsors 20% on their pharmacy benefit costs. They also emphasize the importance of customer experience which reflects in their 99% customer retention rate. ‍ Closing Notes And there you have it! Although small, transparent PBMs are proving to be a powerful player in the industry, turning it on its head with their clear and straightforward approach to managing pharmacy benefits. We hope that in the future this will become the new standard in the industry, yet for that we need to remain patient. In the meantime, we highlighted some standout examples that are leading the charge and showing what’s possible when PBMs prioritize their clients’ needs. So, as you explore your options, keep these top contenders in mind or let us know and we can help! ‍

title: Invoice approvals process: routing, controls, and audit trails
summary: Design an invoice approvals process with routing rules, exception handling, audit trails, escalation paths, and fewer email or spreadsheet handoffs.
body_text: An invoice approvals process is the control workflow that decides whether an invoice is ready for the next finance action. For vendor invoices, that usually means approval before payment. For B2B SaaS customer invoices, it can mean approval before an invoice is sent, adjusted, written off, or escalated. The goal is the same either way: finance needs the right person to review the right context, make the decision on time, and leave enough evidence that the decision still makes sense later. A healthy process is a control system, not a chain of "approve" buttons. It defines routing, exception handling, audit trail requirements, escalation paths, and the systems that must update after the decision. Without that design, approvals turn into email threads, spreadsheet trackers, and Slack direct messages that are fast in the moment but painful during close, collections, reconciliation, or an audit. What an invoice approvals process should do An invoice approvals process should confirm five things before finance releases the invoice or payment: The invoice is legitimate. The amount, terms, customer or vendor, and supporting documents are correct. The right person has authority to approve it. Any exception has a clear owner and resolution path. The decision is recorded in the right system of record. For accounts payable (AP), this protects the company from paying incorrect, duplicate, unsupported, or fraudulent vendor invoices. For accounts receivable (AR), it protects the company from sending customer invoices that do not match the contract, usage data, credits, purchase order requirement, or agreed billing schedule. The control idea is not new. The COSO internal control framework treats approvals, authorizations, verifications, reconciliations, and segregation of duties as core control activities. The GAO Green Book uses similar principles around control activities, documentation, and separating duties so one person does not control the entire flow. In plain finance language: no single person should be able to create, approve, release, and reconcile a risky invoice without another control catching mistakes. The healthy invoice approvals process in 8 steps The exact workflow depends on your systems, but most finance teams need the same basic sequence. Step What happens Control question 1. Intake The invoice enters one controlled queue from email, portal, billing system, enterprise resource planning (ERP), or customer relationship management (CRM). Is every invoice captured once, with a clear owner? 2. Match Finance checks the invoice against the purchase order (PO), receipt, contract, billing schedule, usage data, or customer terms. Does the invoice match the source record? 3. Code and enrich The invoice gets general ledger (GL) coding, department, entity, customer, vendor, project, tax, and payment details. Is the record complete enough to route and post? 4. Route Rules send the invoice to the right approver or approval chain. Who has authority to approve this risk level? 5. Resolve exceptions Mismatches, missing documents, duplicate risk, disputes, or special terms move to an exception owner. What must be fixed before approval? 6. Approve or reject The approver approves, rejects, comments, or sends it back for correction. What was decided, and why? 7. Release the next action The invoice is paid, sent to the customer, adjusted, held, or escalated. Did the decision actually update the workflow? 8. Record and reconcile The decision, documents, and downstream action are logged for reporting, reconciliation, and audit. Can finance prove what happened later? This sequence matters because approval is only one moment in the process. The bigger risk is what happens before and after approval: bad intake, missing context, unclear routing, weak exception ownership, or a decision that never syncs back to the finance system. Book a LedgerUp Demo Build approval routing around risk Approval routing should follow risk, not office politics. If every invoice goes to the CFO, approvals slow down and people rubber-stamp decisions. If too many invoices auto-approve, the process stops being a control. Start with an approval matrix that answers four questions: Who owns the business decision? Who owns the finance control? What dollar amount or risk trigger changes the route? What duties need to stay separated? A useful routing matrix looks something like this. Invoice condition Typical approver Why it needs that route Low-value invoice that matches PO, receipt, and vendor record Auto-approve or AP lead review The source documents already support the payment. Department spend above a threshold Department budget owner The person responsible for the budget confirms business need. Large invoice, new vendor, or unusual payment terms Finance manager or controller Finance reviews cash impact, policy fit, and documentation. Vendor bank-detail change or payment-account change Finance plus independent verification Bank changes are high fraud-risk events and need extra separation. Customer invoice with custom contract terms or usage overage Billing/finance owner The approver confirms the invoice matches the signed terms and usage logic. Credit, write-off, short-pay, or customer dispute Finance leader plus account owner when needed The decision affects revenue, collections, and customer relationship history. Segregation of duties is the part teams often skip. The person who changes vendor payment details should not be the only person approving payment. The person who builds a high-value customer invoice should not be the only person approving a non-standard credit. The person reconciling cash should not be the only person releasing the payment or invoice. Small teams may not have enough people for perfect separation. That is fine if the process adds compensating controls: dual approval on high-risk items, independent review after the fact, system logs, and exception reporting. Design exception handling before invoices get stuck Exceptions are not edge cases. They are the reason approval processes exist. If the process only works when every field is perfect, finance will rebuild the real workflow in side channels. Someone will paste screenshots in Slack, maintain a spreadsheet of stuck invoices, or forward email chains until the right person notices. Define exception types up front and assign each one an owner. Exception Common cause Owner Required resolution Missing PO, receipt, or contract Invoice arrived without supporting documents. Requester, department owner, or deal owner Attach support or reject until support exists. Price, quantity, or usage mismatch Invoice does not match PO, receipt, contract, or usage data. AP, billing operations, or revenue operations (RevOps) Correct source record, correct invoice, or document approved variance. Duplicate invoice risk Same vendor/customer, amount, period, invoice number, or usage period appears twice. AP or billing ops Confirm duplicate status before payment or sending. Master-data change Vendor bank data, billing contact, customer PO, tax, or payment details changed. Finance plus independent verifier Verify the change outside the original request path. Tax, entity, or currency issue Wrong legal entity, tax treatment, or currency. Controller or finance ops Correct coding before release. Customer invoice dispute or short-pay Customer says amount, timing, terms, or service period is wrong. Finance plus account owner Resolve, adjust, collect, or document write-off path. Approval timeout Approver does not respond by the service-level agreement (SLA). Finance queue owner Escalate to backup approver or finance lead. The key is to separate "needs approval" from "needs rework." An approver should not be asked to approve an invoice that is missing basic support. That invoice should enter an exception queue, get fixed, and only then route for a real decision. Set escalation paths that protect cycle time Approval delays are usually process design problems, not personality problems. If approvers do not know what they are approving, where to approve, or what happens after they approve, they will wait. Set escalation rules before the process goes live: Define an SLA by risk level. For example, same business day for invoice send approvals, two business days for routine AP approvals, and immediate escalation for payment holds or customer-facing deadlines. Assign backup approvers for every approval lane. Escalate stale approvals automatically instead of relying on finance to chase people manually. Keep escalation in the controlled workflow, not in private direct messages. Let approvers reject or send back with a reason instead of forcing a yes/no choice. Make the downstream effect clear: pay, send, hold, adjust, cancel, or escalate. The best escalation paths are visible but not noisy. Finance should be able to see every stuck invoice in one place, while approvers receive only the context and reminders they need to make the decision. Make the audit trail useful after approval An audit trail needs more than a timestamp that says "approved." It should explain the decision well enough that someone can understand it weeks or months later. A finance-grade invoice approval log should keep: Audit trail element Why it matters Approver identity and role Shows that the right authority made the decision. Date and time Supports close timing, payment timing, and audit evidence. Context shown to the approver Proves what information the decision was based on. Supporting documents Connects the decision to the PO, receipt, contract, invoice, usage report, or customer request. Decision and comment Captures approve, reject, send back, hold, override, or escalation reason. Field changes before or after approval Shows whether amount, terms, coding, tax, or payment details changed. Exception and escalation history Explains delays, overrides, and rework. Downstream action Confirms the invoice was paid, sent, adjusted, held, or reconciled. This is where email and chat-only approvals fall short. A Slack message can be a great approval surface, but the audit trail needs to live with the invoice record or sync back to the finance system. If your team is tightening controls more broadly, LedgerUp's guide to internal controls in finance goes deeper on how approvals, reconciliations, access controls, and review evidence work together. Where email, spreadsheets, and tool switching break the process Manual invoice approvals feel flexible until volume rises. Then the process breaks in predictable ways. U.S. Bank describes manual AP processes as rooted in paper invoices, email approvals, and fragmented spreadsheets that create silos, reduce visibility, and increase risk. Its summary of 2025 Association for Financial Professionals (AFP) survey findings says manual workflows often take 10-30 minutes per invoice and can cost up to $40 per transaction, depending on complexity and company size. It also cites error and duplicate-payment risk as major consequences of manual AP work. The exact numbers will vary by company, but the pattern is familiar: The invoice lives in one inbox. The contract or PO lives in another system. The approval happens in email or Slack. The exception tracker lives in a spreadsheet. The final payment or invoice-send action happens somewhere else. The audit evidence has to be reconstructed later. Tool switching also creates quiet control gaps. An approver may approve based on a screenshot instead of the live record. A finance analyst may update the spreadsheet but forget the ERP. A rejected invoice may get corrected but never re-routed. A customer dispute may pause collections in someone's notes but not in the system that sends follow-ups. That is why a modern approval process should remove manual handoffs instead of digitizing the old ones. What to automate first Do not start by automating every decision. Start by automating the parts of the process that should not require judgment. The best first targets are: Centralized intake, so every invoice enters one controlled queue. Source matching, so PO, receipt, contract, usage, and billing data are pulled into the record. Rule-based routing, so invoices go to the right approver without finance manually forwarding them. Reminders and escalations, so stale approvals do not depend on a person remembering to chase. Exception queues, so mismatches have owners, due dates, and resolution history. Approval actions in the team's working surface, such as Slack, when the approver has enough context to decide there. System-of-record sync, so the decision updates billing, AP, ERP, CRM, collections, or reconciliation workflows . Reporting, so finance can see approval cycle time, exception rate, overdue approvals, rework, and approval-to-release lag. Human review still matters. The point is to reserve human approval for high-risk or judgment-heavy moments: unusual terms, missing support, large amounts, customer disputes, credits, write-offs, payment-detail changes, and exceptions that could affect revenue or cash. How Ari fits a modern B2B SaaS approval process For B2B SaaS teams, invoice approval is not always about vendor bills. A finance team may need to approve customer invoices before they go out because the invoice depends on contract terms, usage data, discounts, credits, purchase order requirements, or a customer-specific billing schedule. That is where LedgerUp's Ari fits. Ari is LedgerUp's AI revenue teammate for post-signature finance work. Instead of making finance jump between CRM, contracts, billing tools, spreadsheets, email, and Slack, Ari can keep the workflow closer to where the decision happens. Ari reads the contract, billing, and usage context, routes approvals and exceptions in Slack when a human decision is needed, and keeps the downstream contract-to-cash workflow connected. That matters because Slack approval by itself is not the control. The control is the whole path: the invoice is checked against the right contract and billing context, the approver sees the reason approval is required, the invoice is held or released based on the decision, the decision history is preserved, and the follow-up work continues in billing, collections, reconciliation, or customer communication. For the Slack-specific mechanics, see LedgerUp's Slack invoice approval workflow template , Slack invoice approval workflow guide , and Slack integration docs . For the broader revenue workflow, see Meet Ari and LedgerUp's contract-to-cash automation page. Invoice approvals process checklist Use this checklist before you launch or redesign the process. Policy and ownership Define which invoices require approval and which can auto-approve. Separate AP/vendor invoice approvals from AR/customer invoice approvals. Name the finance owner for the overall process. Document who owns business approval, finance approval, exception resolution, and release. Routing rules Set dollar thresholds. Add route changes for new vendors or customers, non-standard terms, credits, write-offs, bank changes, and usage-based charges. Assign backup approvers. Keep duties separated where risk is high. Exception handling Define the exception types. Assign owners and due dates. Decide what evidence is required to clear each exception. Track recurring exception causes so the process improves over time. Escalation paths Set approval SLAs. Automate reminders before approvals become late. Escalate stale approvals to backup owners. Keep escalations visible in the workflow. Audit trail Record who approved, when, why, and with what context. Preserve support documents and field changes. Sync the final decision to the system of record. Make rejected, adjusted, held, and escalated invoices as traceable as approved ones. Metrics Approval cycle time. Overdue approvals. Exception rate. Touchless or auto-approved rate. Rework after rejection. Duplicate invoice rate. Approval-to-payment or approval-to-send lag. A healthy invoice approvals process is easy to describe, hard to bypass, and simple to audit. When finance can answer who approved the invoice, what they saw, why they made the decision, what happened next, and where that evidence lives, the process is doing its job. title: Zenas BioPharma Announces Inducement Grants Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4)
summary: WALTHAM, Mass., July 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Zenas BioPharma, Inc. body_text: Zenas BioPharma Announces Inducement Grants Under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4) July 17, 2026 PDF Version WALTHAM, Mass., July 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Zenas BioPharma, Inc. (“Zenas” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: ZBIO), a clinical-stage global biopharmaceutical company committed to being a leader in the development and commercialization of transformative therapies for patients living with autoimmune diseases, today announced that on July 15, 2026 (the “Grant Date”), the Compensation Committee of the Company’s Board of Directors granted non-qualified stock options to purchase an aggregate of 35,750 shares of the Company’s common stock (“Stock Options”) and an aggregate of 79,050 restricted stock units of the Company’s common stock (“RSUs”) to newly hired employees of the Company as an inducement material to such employees’ entry into employment with the Company, in accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5635(c)(4) (the “Inducement Grant”). The Stock Options have a ten-year term and an exercise price per share of $29.41, which is equal to the closing price of Zenas’ common stock on the Grant Date. The Stock Options will vest over a four-year period, with 25% of the shares vesting on the one-year anniversary of each of the employees’ first day of employment with the Company, and thereafter the remainder of the option will vest in 36 equal monthly installments. The RSUs will vest in four (4) equal installments over a four-year period, with vesting as to twenty-five percent (25%) of the RSUs subject to the award on each of July 15, 2027, July 15, 2028, July 15, 2029 and July 15, 2030. Inducement Grants are subject to the employees’ continued service with Zenas through the applicable vesting dates. The Inducement Grants were granted pursuant to, and are subject to, the terms and conditions of the Company’s 2026 Inducement Plan and the applicable award agreement. About Zenas BioPharma, Inc. Zenas is a clinical-stage global biopharmaceutical company committed to becoming a leader in the development and commercialization of transformative therapies for patients living with autoimmune diseases. Our core business strategy combines our experienced leadership team with a disciplined product candidate acquisition approach to identify, acquire and develop product candidates globally that we believe can provide superior clinical benefits to patients living with autoimmune diseases. Zenas is advancing two late-stage, potential franchise molecules, obexelimab and orelabrutinib. Obexelimab, Zenas’ lead product candidate, is a bifunctional monoclonal antibody designed to bind both CD19 and FcγRIIb, which are broadly present across B cell lineage, to inhibit the activity of cells that are implicated in many autoimmune diseases without depleting them. We believe that obexelimab’s unique mechanism of action and self-administered, subcutaneous injection regimen may broadly and effectively address the pathogenic role of B cell lineage in chronic autoimmune disease. Orelabrutinib is a potentially best-in-class, highly selective CNS-penetrant, oral, small molecule BTK inhibitor. Orelabrutinib’s mechanism of action targets pathogenic B cells not only in the periphery but also within the CNS. Additionally, it directly modulates macrophages and microglial cells in the CNS, with the potential to address compartmentalized inflammation and disease progression in MS. Zenas’ earlier stage programs include ZB021, a novel, potentially best-in-class, oral, IL-17AA/AF inhibitor, ZB022, a preclinical, potentially best-in-class, oral, brain-penetrant, TYK2 inhibitor, and ZB014, a preclinical, half-life extended anti-CD19 and FcγRIIb monoclonal antibody. For more information about Zenas BioPharma, please visit https://zenasbio.com/ and follow us on LinkedIn . body_text: If you're evaluating Retool vs Appsmith for building internal tools, the decision comes down to a fundamental trade-off: enterprise polish and governance versus open-source flexibility and cost control. Both platforms let you build internal apps - dashboards, admin panels, custom CRMs - using drag and drop UI builders, data source integrations, and JavaScript-driven business logic. But they diverge sharply on licensing, pricing structure, deployment access, and how much control you retain over your stack. That difference has real consequences for your development process, long-term operating costs, and ability to scale without surprises. This comparison breaks down exactly where each platform wins, where it falls short, and which one fits your situation - based on current pricing, features, and deployment options as of July 2026. The short answer: Retool is the stronger choice for mid-to-large enterprises that need extensive native integrations, enterprise grade security baked in by default, and polished pre built components to ship internal tools fast - provided budget isn't the primary constraint. Appsmith is the better pick for teams that want an open source solution with full self hosting freedom, deeper customization through custom code, and a more cost effective solution at scale. Both platforms require JavaScript knowledge for basic tasks, so neither is truly no code. What Is Retool? Retool is a proprietary, enterprise-focused low code platform designed to help teams build internal tools quickly using a visual development environment. Its key features include an extensive component library with over 100 UI components, workflow automation capabilities, and over 70 native integrations spanning SQL and NoSQL databases, data warehouses, SaaS tools, and AI providers. Retool is recognized for its strong enterprise governance and compliance posture, including audit logs, granular permission controls, and role based access control out of the box. Retool is highly regarded for a smoother user experience in development, and its documentation makes onboarding easier for developers. What Is Appsmith? Appsmith is an open-source platform under the Apache 2.0 license , built for developers who want maximum control over their internal tool development. Its defining strengths are open-source transparency, extensive use of JavaScript for application logic, a built-in Custom Widget feature for HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and cost-effectiveness - including a free plan that includes unlimited apps for unlimited users. Appsmith supports Git integrations for version management of applications, has a Theme Editor for customizing UI colors and typography, and is designed for flexibility in custom widget development. It's a popular choice for creating customer support systems, admin panels, and data collection tools. Retool vs Appsmith: How They Compare at a Glance Factor Retool Appsmith Best for Enterprises needing fast internal tool delivery, strong governance, many integrations Teams wanting open-source control, self hosting flexibility, cost efficiency Pricing model Per-user: Free (5 users), Team ($10/builder + $5/internal user), Business ($50/builder + $15/internal user), Enterprise (custom) Per-user/flat: Free (unlimited apps/users), Business ($15/user/mo), Enterprise (~$2,500/mo for 100 users) Deployment options Cloud, managed self-hosted, self-hosted (Enterprise only); requires Kubernetes for production Cloud, self-hosted via Docker/Kubernetes (all tiers), air-gapped edition, managed hosting Data sources 70+ native integrations; built in database; managed file/vector storage 25+ databases, REST/GraphQL APIs; premium integrations in paid tiers Security features SSO, RBAC, audit logging, MFA, SOC 2, secrets management - many enforced by default SSO/SAML/OIDC, RBAC, audit logs (Business+), SOC 2, SCIM - requires plan upgrades for full suite Customization React-based custom components; 100+ pre-built UI elements; modules Full JS/HTML/CSS; custom widgets; third party libraries; open source codebase Self-hosting user limit 25-user limit for non-enterprise self hosting No additional usage limits for self-hosted customers The headline takeaway: Retool offers more out-of-the-box enterprise readiness, while Appsmith gives you more freedom and lower entry costs - especially for self hosted solutions. Data Layer and Integrations For internal tools, the ability to connect to your existing data sources - databases, APIs, third party services - is non-negotiable. A platform with weak connectors forces you to write custom apis and middleware, slowing the entire development process. Retool provides over 70 native integrations for databases and APIs, covering PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, DynamoDB, BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, Google Sheets, and more. It also ships with a built in database for lightweight data storage and managed file storage, which means you can prototype internal apps without provisioning external infrastructure. Retool offers connections to AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini) and includes schema browsing, query editors, and connection pooling. Appsmith supports 25+ databases and any REST or GraphQL API. It handles the major SQL and NoSQL tools well, but its premium integrations - connectors for specific third party platforms - are gated behind Business and Enterprise plans. For teams that primarily work with standard databases and custom apis, Appsmith covers the essentials. But if you need deep, managed connectivity to data warehouses, SaaS platforms, or AI services without writing glue code, Retool's catalog is broader. Both platforms can create custom CRMs and dashboards, and both let you write queries directly against connected data sources. Appsmith supports building admin panels and data collection tools with the same connector set. Winner: Retool - Its integration count, built in database, and managed data layer features give it a clear edge for teams with diverse data source integrations. Appsmith is sufficient for standard database and API connectivity but requires more manual work for less common third party integrations. Customization and Development Experience How deeply you can customize your internal applications - and how pleasant the process is - directly affects long-term tool effectiveness and developer adoption. Retool offers over 100 pre-built components for app development across its UI builder, including tables, charts, forms, modals, maps, and input controls. Retool allows importing custom React components for app customization, so teams already working in React can extend the platform naturally. Its visual development approach, combined with JavaScript for business logic, balances speed with flexibility. Retool is easier for developers due to its documentation, and it offers extensive third-party courses for learning. However, building outside what Retool supports may require workarounds - the core platform is proprietary, and deep deviations from its component model can be friction-heavy. Appsmith provides a built-in Custom Widget feature for HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, giving technical users full control over every UI element. Appsmith allows extensive use of JavaScript for application logic, and you can import third party libraries freely. Its developer experience is more "code-first" - you're closer to the underlying HTML/CSS/JS, which gives you more power but demands more technical expertise. Appsmith has a Theme Editor for customizing UI colors and typography, and version control via Git with custom branches makes collaborative development workflows natural. Appsmith's learning curve is less steep than Retool's for developers comfortable with JavaScript, though Appsmith may require more configuration efforts for complex applications. Both platforms support third-party libraries for enhanced functionality, and both require JavaScript knowledge for basic tasks. The trade-off is clear: Retool's component library is richer and more polished; Appsmith's approach gives you more raw control. Winner: Appsmith for deep customization and developer control - its open-source codebase, custom widgets, and full JS/HTML/CSS access give developers more freedom. Retool wins on speed and polish - its pre built components and guided UI builder get you to a working app faster with less custom code. Choose based on whether your team values flexibility or velocity. Security, Governance, and Auditability Internal tools often handle sensitive operational data - customer records, financial information, infrastructure access. Enterprise grade security isn't optional; it's a requirement. Retool features include audit logging and granular permission controls, with RBAC, SSO (SAML/OIDC), secrets management, multi-factor authentication, and workspace isolation available across Business and Enterprise plans. Retool is recommended for enterprise applications requiring robust security features, and its governance model enforces security policies by default - reducing the risk that someone builds retool apps without proper access controls. Both platforms are SOC 2 certified, but Retool's compliance posture (including GDPR) is more prominently documented and enforced at lower plan tiers. Retool is recognized for its strong enterprise governance and compliance. Appsmith offers role based access control, SSO via OAuth and SAML, SCIM user provisioning, and audit logs - but these features are largely gated to Business and Enterprise tiers. Appsmith supports two factor authentication and claims SOC 2, HIPAA, and GDPR compliance in its commercial offerings. The air-gapped edition (Enterprise) addresses strict isolation requirements. However, governance in Appsmith is more configurable than automatic - you need to set up the right policies, especially in self-hosted deployments. Both platforms support OAuth and SAML authentication. Both provide self-hosted deployment options for organizations that need data to stay within their virtual private cloud. Winner: Retool - Its security features are more comprehensive at lower tiers, and governance is enforced by default rather than requiring manual configuration. Appsmith can achieve similar outcomes but needs more setup and higher-tier plans to match. For regulated industries, Retool's track record (used by enterprises like Brex and Adobe with reported zero security incidents across 100+ apps) provides additional confidence. Deployment and Infrastructure Deployment flexibility matters because organizations have vastly different requirements - from cloud-first startups to air-gapped government environments. Both Retool and Appsmith offer self-hosted deployment options. Retool supports deployment on Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, and Azure, and also offers a cloud-hosted option and managed self-hosted infrastructure. However, a critical change as of 2025–2026: Retool now restricts self-hosting to its Enterprise plan for new customers. Retool imposes a 25-user limit for non-enterprise self hosting. Self-hosted Retool 4.0 requires Kubernetes with Helm charts, plus supporting services (agent sandbox, JS executor, MCP server), making the infrastructure overhead significant. Appsmith can be self-hosted using Docker and Kubernetes across all tiers, including the free Community edition. Self-hosted Appsmith customers face no additional usage limits. Best practices for production recommend a t3.medium instance (sufficient for hundreds of users), separate node groups, and Kubernetes for high availability. Appsmith also offers an air-gapped edition and managed hosting on dedicated servers in its Enterprise plan. For infrastructure costs, Appsmith shifts more responsibility to the user - you supply compute, storage, backups, and monitoring. Retool's Enterprise self-hosted option provides more packaged support but at a significantly higher price point. Winner: Appsmith - Self hosting is available from the free tier up, with no user limits and lighter infrastructure requirements. Retool's restriction of self-hosting to Enterprise only is a significant constraint for teams that want on-premises deployment without enterprise-level spend. Pricing Model and Total Cost of Ownership Pricing structure can make or break platform economics as your team grows. The way each platform charges has material implications beyond the sticker price. Retool's free plan allows up to 5 users, with 500 workflow runs/month and 5 GB each of database capacity and file storage. Paid plans start at $10/builder/month + $5/internal user on the Team plan, rising to $50/builder + $15/internal user on the Business plan. Retool charges $8 per external user per month. Enterprise pricing is custom. Retool is typically more expensive due to its per-user pricing model, and the builder-vs-user distinction can create unexpected cost escalation as adoption grows. Custom branding, portals, and embedding are Business plan and above features. Appsmith's free plan includes unlimited apps for unlimited users (self-hosted) or up to 5 users on cloud. Appsmith's Business plan starts at $15 per user per month, adding unlimited workspaces, premium integrations, audit logs, and priority support. Appsmith's paid plans start at $40 per month for 100 hours of usage on certain workflow-based tiers. Enterprise runs approximately $2,500/month for 100 users, including SSO, SCIM, managed hosting, and the air-gapped edition. Appsmith is suited for startups looking for cost-effective solutions. The total cost of ownership diverges further when you factor in self hosting infrastructure. Appsmith's free version lets you run production workloads on your own hardware with no license fee. Retool requires Enterprise-tier licensing for any self-hosted deployment, making the minimum self-hosted cost substantially higher. Winner: Appsmith for cost-sensitive teams and smaller organizations - its free version is genuinely usable in production, and per-user costs scale more predictably. Retool may deliver better TCO for large enterprises that would otherwise spend engineering time building the integrations, governance, and workflow automation that Retool includes natively in its enterprise plan. Production Readiness and Performance A platform that works in demos but struggles under real workloads is a liability for business-critical internal tools. Retool has invested heavily in production readiness, releasing Self-hosted Retool 4.0 with a rebuilt React-based app builder, real-time collaborative editing, agent sandboxing, and performance improvements. It's used in large enterprises to power 100+ internal applications, with query execution metadata, observability tooling, and staging-vs-production resource separation. Retool's workflow automation handles high-concurrency scenarios, and its integration with data warehouses (Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery) supports heavy analytical workloads. Appsmith is production-ready and used by many organizations - GSK reportedly built an app to patch 3,500 Linux servers in a single sprint, and HeyJobs claims to add new features 90% faster using the platform. Appsmith's self-hosting best practices provide operational guidance for HA setups, hardware sizing, and component separation. However, at very large scale or with complex UIs rendering large datasets, Appsmith may need more infrastructure tuning and custom optimization. The component library, while flexible, is less polished than Retool's for building web apps with complex multi screen apps. Both platforms require JavaScript knowledge for basic tasks, and performance in both cases depends heavily on the underlying data sources and infrastructure. Winner: Retool - Its enterprise track record, built-in observability, and recent 4.0 infrastructure improvements give it an edge for production workloads at scale. Appsmith is production-capable and performant for most use cases but places more infrastructure responsibility on your ops team. Retool vs Appsmith: Which Should You Choose? Choose Retool if you're an enterprise or mid-large team with diverse data sources, need for strong governance and audit logs enforced by default, want the fastest path to building web apps with polished UI elements, and have the budget for per-user pricing. Retool is especially strong when you need extensive native integrations, workflow automation, and security features that satisfy compliance teams without extensive configuration. Choose Appsmith if your organization values open-source transparency, wants to self-host without enterprise-tier licensing, has developers comfortable with JavaScript and custom code, and prioritizes cost control over out-of-box polish. Appsmith is the clear choice for startups, budget-conscious teams, and organizations that want to avoid vendor lock-in. Appsmith emphasizes open-source benefits and avoiding vendor lock-in. Consider Jet Admin if neither platform fully fits. Jet Admin builds secure business apps on existing data - it connects to existing databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools, generates the interface and application/backend logic, then deploys the app to users. It's worth evaluating as a third option, particularly if you want a platform that combines visual development with production-grade deployment without the pricing complexity of Retool or the infrastructure overhead of self-hosted Appsmith. There is no universal winner in the appsmith vs retool comparison. The right choice depends on your team's technical expertise, budget, compliance requirements, and how much control you want over the underlying stack. Frequently Asked Questions Can you migrate between Retool and Appsmith? Migration between the two platforms is non-trivial. There is no automated tool that converts retool apps to Appsmith or vice versa. UI components, query logic, workflows, and custom components all require re-implementation. Your data layer (databases, APIs) can usually be reused since both platforms connect to the same data sources, but presentation logic, permissions, and governance configuration need manual mapping. Plan for a full rebuild of the front-end layer rather than a straightforward migration. Which platform is better for large enterprises? Retool is the stronger choice for large enterprises. Its additional features - enforced RBAC, audit logging with query metadata, SSO/SCIM, workspace isolation, and compliance certifications - are available and active at lower friction than Appsmith's equivalent features, which require Business or Enterprise tier upgrades and more manual configuration. Retool also has a deeper track record with enterprise customers in regulated industries. However, Appsmith's Enterprise plan can meet most enterprise requirements, particularly for organizations that prioritize open-source and self hosting. How do self-hosting requirements compare? Both platforms support self hosting via Docker and Kubernetes. Appsmith's self-hosted Community edition runs on a single t3.medium instance supporting hundreds of users, with no licensing cost and no usage limits. Retool's self-hosted option now requires an Enterprise plan, uses Kubernetes with Helm charts, and involves multiple services (agent sandbox, JS executor, etc.) - making infrastructure setup more complex and costly. If self hosting is a priority, Appsmith offers a significantly lower barrier to entry. Which offers better long-term vendor lock-in protection? Appsmith, as an open source solution under Apache 2.0, provides stronger protection against vendor lock-in. The source code is transparent, and community forks are possible. Retool is proprietary - once you're deeply embedded with its custom components, workflows, and core functionality, switching costs are high. That said, both platforms create some degree of lock-in through platform-specific UI logic and integrations; the key differences are in licensing and the ability to inspect or modify the platform itself. Is either platform suitable for citizen developers or non-technical users? Both platforms lean toward technical users rather than citizen developers. Both require JavaScript knowledge for basic tasks like writing queries, defining business logic, and configuring data transformations. Retool's more polished drag and drop UI builder and pre built components make it somewhat more accessible to semi-technical users, while Appsmith's code-first approach is better suited to developers comfortable with JavaScript and version control. Neither is a true no code platform. Can these platforms handle external users and customer-facing apps? Yes, with caveats. Retool supports external users through portals and embedded apps, charging $8 per external user per month on eligible plans. Appsmith offers private app embedding in its Enterprise tier. Both platforms were designed primarily for creating internal tools rather than building web apps for public-facing use, so while customer-facing use cases are possible, they may involve minor variations in branding, authentication, and performance optimization compared to purpose-built front-end frameworks. Evaluating more options beyond Retool and Appsmith? Jet Admin lets you build secure internal applications on your existing data sources - try it free to see how it compares.

title: How to turn flat lay photos into on-model images for e‑commerce
summary: Learn how to turn flat lay photos into on-model images for cost-effective, conversion-ready e‑commerce fashion listings at catalog scale.
body_text: Flat lay photos are a practical way for small and mid-size businesses to photograph clothing catalogs. One overhead setup can cover an entire product line, and these images show the item’s color and design details clearly, which is critical for selling soft goods like clothing and accessories online. But they don’t show how the garment falls on a body, and traditional shoots with fashion models require more production time and a much larger budget. On-model images provide the necessary context to help buyers picture themselves wearing the clothes. In this guide, we’ll walk through how to turn flat lay photos into on-model images, so budding fashion brands and e‑commerce sellers can create catalog-ready visuals from the assets they already have. Throughout, we’ll explore how Photoroom’s Batch edit capabilities, alongside Flat Lay and AI Virtual Model tools, help small teams convert those images at scale. Table of contents: What’s “flat lay to on-model” photography, and why do teams use it? How to turn a flat lay into an on-model image in 6 steps Turn flat lays into a scalable on-model workflow Frequently asked questions What’s “flat lay to on-model” photography, and why do teams use it? Converting a flat lay to an on-model image puts an existing top-down garment photo into context by dressing a model with the item. Flat lay shots are important for online catalogs because they display details like stitch quality and overall garment shape, while on-model images help buyers judge the fit, length, and overall silhouette. Teams turn flat lay images into model photos for several reasons. Higher trust, lower return rates Finding a cute shirt or nice pair of low-rise jeans in an online storefront is one thing, but understanding how the shirt’s fabric drapes or where the jeans sit makes a bigger impact on a buyer’s purchase decision. Since e‑commerce shoppers can’t physically try on clothing, it’s important that they can see the product in context by putting it on a body. Buyers who can see how a garment could fit via an on-model image are more likely to visualize how that fit will translate on their body. That stronger visualization means they’ll have higher trust in the clothes they’re buying, and you’ll see fewer returns after delivery. Show the cut when worn A flat lay can show that a shirt has dropped shoulders, but it doesn’t reveal where the shoulder seam falls or where the hem lands when someone wears it. On-model product photography makes those proportions visible and demonstrates how the material behaves. For example, a structured blazer keeps a firm line, while a soft dress falls closer to the body. This way, shoppers get realistic information about the silhouette before they place an order. Display fit on different body types Flat lays show the general shape of an item, but shoppers may struggle to picture that shape against their own proportions. Only using one model also gives a limited view when a brand serves customers with a range of body types. Photoroom lets teams generate the same apparel on pre-set AI fashion models with a range of body types without booking a separate shoot for each one. You can also upload your own model images, which are saved in Brand Kit so your team can use the same model for catalog continuity in later product drops. Add on-model shots after the campaign shoot A campaign fashion photography shoot can only cover the products brought to set that day. When last-minute product additions miss the shoot, the team must book another session or publish a product listing with fewer useful images. A flat lay to model workflow starts with the inventory photos the team already has. Fashion sellers can create an on-model image with just a phone, natural lighting, and a clean background, even when the official shoot has wrapped. Scale on-model photography without losing consistency A production team can keep one photoshoot visually consistent. The challenge starts when a growing catalog requires different photographers and locations, or when edits stretch over longer periods of time and editors join and leave the team. All of these small changes introduce variations in your images, which makes your catalog look disconnected. Inconsistent catalogs, in turn, lower customers’ confidence that what they see is what they’ll get. Flat lay to model gives teams more control over the process. They can photograph every garment with the same flat lay setup, then use Photoroom to place each item on the same AI fashion model. Teams can also reuse the approved pose and background broadly across up to 250 SKUs with Photoroom’s Batch edit feature, so new additions stay visually consistent without another round of creative alignment. Enterprise teams can extend the same workflow on a larger catalog through existing workflows using the AI Fashion Model API . For example, Marketplace GoodBuy Gear increased conversion rates by 23% after adopting Photoroom’s API. How to turn a flat lay into an on-model image in 6 steps Producing on-model images through traditional photoshoots requires extensive budget planning and collaborations, especially when catalogs grow. Photoroom combines bulk image preparation with virtual AI models for e‑commerce in one platform, so teams can turn existing assets into on-model visuals while reducing editing costs, like the marketplace Selency did . Here’s how to use Photoroom to turn flat lays into on-model images in just six steps. 1. Upload and prepare your flat lay Open Photoroom and upload a sharp image that shows the complete garment. If you’re starting from an existing product image, select “Flat Lay,” then add any specifications like image size or styles from your Brand Kit. Once you have a flat lay image ready in Photoroom (directly uploaded or created via the Flat Lay tool), you can use integrated editing tools like AI Background Remover to remove the original background when it blends into the clothing or adds clutter around the edges and Edit with AI to make changes through text prompts. If wrinkles distort the outline, use the Ironing tool to smooth them without flattening every natural fold. 2. Open AI Fashion Models From your Photoroom Space, select AI Fashion Models. You’ll need to pick at least one image to start, but if you’d like to display more than one item on a model at a time, you can add up to four total at this stage. Listings that need a product-focused image without a visible person should use AI Ghost Mannequin to create an invisible-mannequin view from a flat lay or hanger shot. You’ll skip steps three and four, but the rest are similar for both tools. 3. Choose a preset or custom model Select a model from Photoroom’s preset library. You can also upload custom model photography that matches your existing campaign. Photoroom saves all models in AI Fashion Model and can add them to your Brand Kit , which makes it easier for other team members to reference and use the same model later. Photoroom’s library includes 12 models with different body types and skin tones. Including a range of appearances emphasizes inclusivity and gives more shoppers relevant body references across the collection, ultimately supporting higher conversion potential from a broader audience. According to the Unstereotype Alliance’s 2026 report , created in partnership with Oxford University’s business school, brands who used inclusive models found about 3.5% higher short-term conversion rates and 16% in the long term. 4. Set the pose and background Choose a pose from Photoroom’s list that keeps the apparel visible , such as a hand in pocket for a blouse or arms crossed for jeans, then select a background or upload your own (including images you’ve already generated in Photoroom, or new images you’d like to create). Alongside these generation settings, you can also use text prompts to refine the model’s position or crop , such as showing only the upper half of the model, to minimize the number of edits you have to make later. 5. Select the image size and quality Pick an aspect ratio that matches the platform where you plan to publish the on-model image. Some marketplaces require specific aspect ratios, like 16:9, while others have pixel minimums, such as a 500px minimum on the longest side. Don’t worry about matching every marketplace requirement at once—you can use Photoroom’s Batch edit interface to automatically resize and reformat up to 250 images at a time. Finally, select the output quality. Many major marketplaces recommend at least 1,000 x 1,000 pixel resolutions, but Photoroom can generate images in resolutions up to 4K for products that need sharper textures or larger zoom views. 6. Generate, review, and set up batch processing Select “Generate” to get your on-model image. Before exporting, compare the original flat lay to model AI output. Check the color and fit first, then review details such as logos or prints, zippers and buttons, and tags. Once you feel confident with your result, use Batch edits to apply the same AI generated model and setup across multiple product images and lookbooks. You can add identical edits on up to 250 images at a time for a consistent catalog, no matter what listing you’re looking at. Batch processing cuts a lot of time off your editing process, too. When Italian art marketplace intOndo started using Photoroom’s Batch mode, they saved 25 minutes for every 100 images edited—equivalent to 125 hours across their 30,000-item catalog. Turn flat lays into a scalable on-model workflow On-model images help shoppers understand how the apparel fits and falls on the body, which gives them more confidence to click “Purchase.” Traditional photoshoots with models provide those details, but they add more production days and higher costs every time the catalog expands. Photoroom turns existing flat lays into on-model images in seconds—no reshoot necessary. Choose an inclusive and versatile AI fashion model, set the visual direction, and reuse it across all your SKUs with Batch mode. The result is a faster production workflow that keeps new product images on-brand as the catalog grows .

title: AvePoint Fly Server: The Only Migration Solution with a DISA STIG
summary: Simplify security reviews with AvePoint Fly Server, the only migration solution with a DISA STIG for regulated and compliance-driven industries.
body_text: For many enterprise migrations, the security review is where momentum slows. When a migration platform does not come with a recognized security baseline, approvals can take longer, procurement becomes more complex, and deployment in secure environments faces added scrutiny. AvePoint Fly Server changes that equation. The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) has published the official Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) for AvePoint Fly Server, making it the only data migration solution with a dedicated, government-published STIG. It is now live on the DISA Cyber Exchange. It is now live on the DISA Cyber Exchange . Why This Matters Outside Government DISA STIGs provide product-specific hardening guidance that security teams can review against their own requirements. For organizations in finance, healthcare, energy, and other regulated industries, a published STIG gives security and procurement stakeholders a more structured baseline to evaluate — helping them move through review with greater clarity and confidence. It is more than a compliance marker. It gives procurement stakeholders a more structured baseline to evaluate. Three Ways This Changes Your Next Approval Cycle For security, procurement, and IT stakeholders, a published STIG can make the approval cycle more structured and easier to navigate. Here are three practical ways that changes the conversation: 1. Reduces open-ended security review work. Your risk team stops investigating from zero. The exact database, encryption, and system-hardening configuration is pre-documented and published by DISA. You answer their questions before they ask them. 2. Supports deployment in highly secure environments. The validated baseline enforces TLS 1.3, limits non-essential system exposures, and maps role-based access control (RBAC) to NIST SP 800-53 controls. It's built to run inside the most locked-down networks on the planet. 3. Strengthens the case for adoption with recognized validation. Drop the official DISA download link on your security team's desk. The conversation shifts from “prove this tool is safe" to “this tool is already validated by DISA.” Already Running Fly Server? The STIG for Fly Server expands what secure deployment can look like for existing Fly Server environments. With a United States Department of Defense (DoD)-recognized baseline now in place, organizations can: Expand into regulated business units that previously required a separate, pre-approved tool. Pass audits faster with ready-made official compliance checklists. Justify continued investment with a security credential no competing migration product can match. title: Red Cat’s Teal Drones Advances to Gauntlet II of Drone Dominance Program

(Nasdaq: RCAT) (“Red Cat” or the “Company”), a U.S.-based provider of advanced all-domain drone and robotic solutions for defense and national security, today announced that Teal Drones Inc. has advanced to Gauntlet II of the Drone Dominance Program. According to the program’s Phase 2 participant list, Teal is among 19 companies invited to participate in Gauntlet II at Fort Carson, Colorado, in August 2026, following the Phase 2 Qualifier. The Phase 2 Qualifier was held at Camp Grayling, Michigan, where 49 companies were invited to compete and approximately 79 unique drones were tested across Long Range Strike and Tactical Assault in Close Quarters mission areas. Teal’s advancement reflects Red Cat’s continued focus on delivering trusted, mission-ready drone and robotic solutions that support the warfighter with critical situational awareness and operational advantage. “Advancing to Gauntlet II is an honor and a meaningful validation of the work our Teal team is doing to deliver trusted, mission-ready systems for the warfighter,” said Jeff Thompson, CEO of Red Cat. “The Drone Dominance Program is focused on rapidly identifying proven drone technologies that can provide a decisive advantage on the modern battlefield, and we are proud to continue competing in support of that mission.” About Red Cat Holdings, Inc.
